_soak.purpose: 72-hour unattended baseline. Countermeasures OFF on purpose: you cannot measure a leak while something is periodically resetting it, and memoryLimitMb must come from this run rather than a guess.
_soak.geometry: The display is a 4K panel, 3840x2160 LANDSCAPE, at 200% scaling, so the app is handed a 1920x1080 logical window. Authored at 1920x1080 so wall.scale is 1.0 and no layout scaling distorts the panels. NOTE: the first (abandoned) run found this same panel mounted in PORTRAIT at 2160x3840 and was authored at 1080x1920. It was rotated back to landscape between the two runs by the project that owns the machine. The config follows the display rather than the other way round: rotating a shared machine's screen is exactly the kind of unannounced interference that ended the first run.
_soak.why_this_is_still_representative: At 200% scaling Chromium rasterises that window at device pixel ratio 2, so the real raster is 3840x2160 = 8.29 megapixels, which is what drives raster memory and GPU load. That is identical to the portrait mounting the first run used (2160x3840 is the same 8.29 megapixels) and identical to a 3840x2160 wall, so the memory series is comparable across both runs. Landscape is in fact a closer match to a real LED wall than the portrait mounting was: the aspect caveat that applied to the first run does not apply here.
_soak.arms: soak-static is the control and must stay flat. soak-heavy is bounded-by-construction load. The two public panels are realistic but not actionable: if they grow and the local arms do not, the leak is in a third-party page, not in Wallwright.
_soak.threshold_basis: 31.6GB machine. 15 MB/hour is roughly 5GB over three weeks. Judged on the FINAL 24 HOURS, not the whole run: Chromium legitimately climbs for hours before it settles, so an early fit measures warm-up. Pre-registered before T0.
